implementation_notes: C++ gives the best tooling for the measure step: perf, Google Benchmark, and the compiler itself reporting what it did (-fopt-info-vec, -fopt-info-inline) so you can see which loops vectorised and which calls inlined before guessing. The micro-optimisations that pay at a measured hotspot are layout (SoA, contiguous storage, alignment), removing allocations (reserve, small-object), avoiding virtual dispatch in a hot loop, and hoisting. The C++-specific trap is abstraction tax: a virtual call, an iterator, or a shared_ptr in a hot loop costs real cycles that the compiler cannot remove, and -O2 will not fix them - but the fix (devirtualise, use a value, use a raw span) is a design change that hurts readability, which is exactly the trade this pattern requires you to measure and justify.
idiom_name: perf plus Google Benchmark and -fopt-info-vec/-fopt-info-inline, applied at the measured hotspot; layout and allocation as the usual wins
pitfalls: Hand-optimising what -O2 already did: check -fopt-info-inline and -fopt-info-vec before adding a manual inline or unrolling.
The abstraction tax is real but the fix hurts readability: devirtualising, swapping shared_ptr for a value, or using a raw span is a design change - measure to justify it.
False sharing: two hot fields in adjacent structs ping-pong between cores, which no single-threaded benchmark will ever show - test the multithreaded case.
Google Benchmark's default reports a variance; a change inside the confidence interval is not a win and will not reproduce.
reserve() on a hot container: the reallocation is amortised O(1) but the copy is a one-off spike that a short benchmark may attribute to the wrong line.
